Washington, D.C. — This week, the House of Representatives passed the Stop Secret Spending Act, bipartisan legislation Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander (NH-02) helped lead to force the federal government to disclose billions of dollars in spending currently kept off the public books. Goodlander is one of the original cosponsors of the bill and has been a leading voice in Congress for cracking down on corruption and making every federal dollar traceable by the people who pay for it: American taxpayers.

“Public service is a public trust, and the American people have a right to know how every taxpayer dollar is being spent,” said Congresswoman Goodlander. “I am proud to be building a bipartisan coalition in Congress dedicated to a commonsense idea: end secret government spending. Sunlight is the best disinfectant in the fight to crack down on corruption, and our bill will stop secret spending by closing loopholes and giving independent watchdogs the tools they need to hold government accountable. I won’t quit until we get this bill signed into law.”

Last year, the federal government spent a total of $7 trillion taxpayer dollars, and billions of dollars were secretly spent. For example, at the Department of Defense alone, the Government Accountability Office identified $77.5 billion in secret spending between fiscal years 2021 and 2025 that were never reported to USAspending.gov.

This secret spending has been made possible in part by legally binding arrangements outside standard government contracts, grants, and cooperative agreements known as Other Transaction Agreements, or OTAs. OTAs can help the federal government move quickly and work with new partners, but are exempt from many federal procurement laws and requirements. That exemption has created a loophole that allows agencies to hide billions of dollars in spending from USAspending.gov — leaving taxpayers and Congress in the dark about their money is going and why.

The bipartisan bill Goodlander helped lead would require the Department of the Treasury to ensure OTA data is automatically transmitted to USAspending.gov and presented in a centralized view. The Treasury would also publish an annual report identifying the total amount of federal-award spending that has not been posted and explaining why the data remains unavailable. For 10 years after enactment, Inspectors General at specified agencies would periodically assess the quality of agency spending data and compliance with federal data standards.

The Stop Secret Spending Act is led by Congressman Barry Moore (R-AL), and Congressman Jimmy Panetta (D-CA) with Goodlander as an original cosponsor.

The bill advanced unanimously out of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform by a vote of 40 to 0 before passing the full House. Companion legislation led by Senator Joni Ernst (R-IA) passed the Senate unanimously earlier this year.

Goodlander has made cracking down on corruption and cleaning up government a central focus of her work in Congress:

Goodlander is leading the bipartisan Public Service Accountability Act to close ethics loopholes and prohibit senior officials across all three branches of government from trading individual stocks or participating in prediction markets.

Goodlander has repeatedly pushed for greater accountability and transparency at the Pentagon so taxpayers can see how their money is being spent. As a Member of the House Armed Services Committee, she is leading oversight and legislative efforts to force the Department of Defense to conduct and pass a full independent audit,press Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and senior Pentagon officials on the Pentagon’s audit failures and delayed budget, and securing provisions in the National Defense Authorization Act strengthening oversight of Pentagon financial systems and moving the department closer to a clean audit.

She has worked across party lines to bring greater accountability and competition to Pentagon contracting and stop corporate restrictions from wasting taxpayer dollars. Shehelped secure a new system to track defense contractors’ compliance with repair-data requirements, helped introduce the bipartisanWarrior Right to Repair Act of 2025, andco-led a bipartisan amendment adopted by the House Armed Services Committee to strengthen the military’s ability to repair its own equipment.

Goodlander has used independent oversight, legislation, and the courts to challenge waste and unauthorized government spending. Shejoined a call for an Inspector General investigation after the State Department destroyed taxpayer-funded emergency food and millions of dollars’ worth of contraceptives; helped introduce theStrengthening Uniform Procedures to Prevent Loss, Incineration, and Expiration of Supplies (SUPPLIES) Act to prevent similar waste; andjoined a legal brief challenging a proposed $400 million White House ballroom that Congress had neither authorized nor funded.

Goodlander has fought to ensure that Members of Congress are held accountable to the same people they serve. She cosponsored the bipartisanCLEAN Act, which would make the Office of Congressional Ethics permanent;asked the House to withhold her own salary during a government shutdown; and cosponsored the bipartisanNo Pay for Congress During Default or Shutdown Act, which would prevent lawmakers from being paid when Congress fails to fund the government.

Goodlander is a champion for small businesses and is a cosponsor of the Transparency and Predictability in Small Business Opportunities Act, requiring greater disclosure when federal contracting opportunities for small businesses are canceled. The House passed the legislation.

###
title: Goodlander-Backed Bipartisan Bill to Crack Down on Corruption and Expose Billions in Secret Federal Spending Passes the House

Toledo, OH — Today, Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09) announced $1.3 Million in United States Department of Justice awards for Legal Aid of Western Ohio (LAWO) based in Toledo. LAWO works to ensure that the most vulnerable people in our communities have the same access to legal resources as those who can hire an attorney. The non-profit’s Training and Services to End Abuse in Later Life will receive $700,000 to support victims of abuse over the age of 50 and for the professionals that serve them. The Disability Grant Program will receive $600,000 to provide legal advocacy and consultations for abuse victims with disabilities. Both awards will be administered through the Office on Violence Against Women.

“For over a half century, legal aid organizations in our Northwest Ohio community have worked tirelessly to bring well-deserved justice and empowerment to those who need it most,” said Congresswoman Kaptur (OH-09). “I am proud to have helped secure these funds for the Legal Aid of Western Ohio to support victims of abuse and violence. Older individuals and people with disabilities face a higher risk of abuse and often have difficulty finding the resources to get help. LAWO provides much-needed relief to these victims and the professionals who investigate crimes of abuse. They can now build upon existing advocacy efforts and continue to reach people across the nearly three dozen counties they serve.”

LAWO serves individuals and families who demonstrate financial need and require legal advocacy, consultation, or representation. In 2022 alone, the organization closed 4,252 cases to protect and stabilize more than 12,000 low-income individuals in Northwest and Western Ohio. The cases ranged from housing and consumer issues to bankruptcy and education equity. LAWO offers specialized programs for domestic violence survivors and seniors. One DOJ award will specifically address the intersection of these two groups, training criminal justice professionals and other professionals who work with older victims of abuse to create safer communities. The funds will target investigation, prosecution, and victim support services for domestic violence, sexual assault, economic abuse, neglect, stalking, and abandonment against individuals aged 50 or older.

LAWO’s disability program will use its award to provide training, consultation, and information on domestic violence, dating violence, stalking, sexual assault, and abuse by caregivers against individuals with disabilities and Deaf people. People with disabilities are three times as likely to be sexually assaulted than people without disabilities, and there can be many barriers to receiving legal assistance. Increased funding will enhance direct services already provided to these individuals.

# # #
title: Kaptur Announces $1.3 Million in DOJ Awards to Secure Justice for Victims of Abuse and Violence

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Representative Seth Magaziner (RI-02) announced that the United States Tour Operators Association (USTOA) has endorsed his Protected Time Off Act, legislation that would guarantee paid vacation time for workers nationwide.

The endorsement from USTOA, a professional trade association representing tour operators across the country, reflects the growing and broad-based support for ensuring that every worker has a guarantee to paid time off.

“Americans work hard, and they deserve time to recharge,” said Magaziner. “I am grateful for the United States Tour Operators Association’s support for our widely popular effort to guarantee paid time off for every worker. Expanding paid vacation to all workers will not only guarantee fairness for the millions of workers who get no vacation, but it will also give more Americans the opportunity to experience the destinations that make our country so special.”

"The United States Tour Operators Association (USTOA) is proud to support the PTO Act and Congressman Magaziner's efforts to provide paid leave to all Americans," said Jeff Roy, Chairman of USTOA. "Providing paid time off is a win-win for Americans who will get the opportunity to travel with their families and for the local communities around the country whose economies depend on travel and tourism. USTOA strongly urges Congress to expeditiously pass this critical piece of legislation."

The legislation is also endorsed by the AFL-CIO, American Federation of Teachers (AFT), National Education Association (NEA), SMART (International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail and Transportation Workers), Service Employees International Union (SEIU), UNITE HERE, Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU), Center forLaw and Social Policy, Economic Opportunity Institute, Economic Policy Institute, Family Values @ Work, National Employment Law Project, National Partnership for Women and Families, National Women’s Law Center, Paid Leave for All, UnidosUS, and ZERO TO THREE.

BACKGROUND:

The PTO Act was reintroduced in July of 2025 by Magaziner alongside Reps. Nikki Budzinski (IL-13), Greg Casar (TX-35), and Jasmine Crockett (TX-30) to guarantee paid vacation time for all workers. The bill has 83 additional cosponsors.

The PTO Act:

Provide all employees with guaranteed paid vacation time, usable for any reason and paid at their regular wage. Full-time workers will earn a minimum of two weeks of paid vacation per year.

This leave will be in addition to any paid sick leave or family and medical leave that workers already have.

Protect employees against discrimination for exercising their right to take annual paid time off.

More than 27 million private-sector workers in the United States, over one in five, receive no paid vacation at all (source).

The United States is the only advanced economy nation in the world that doesn’t guarantee any paid vacation forworkers. By contrast, the European Union guarantees workers at least 20 paid vacation days per year, with some countries mandating as many as 25 or 30 annual days off.
title: Support for Magaziner’s PTO Act Earns Endorsement from U.S. Tour Operators

WASHINGTON, DC (July 24, 2026) — Yesterday, Congresswoman Valerie Foushee (NC-04) introduced the Stop Prison Price Gouging Act of 2026, legislation to prevent federal prison commissaries from charging prices above fair market value, strengthen oversight of Bureau of Prisons (BOP) contracts, and protect incarcerated people and their families from unfair costs.

The bill would require the Director of the Federal Bureau of Prisons to set commissary prices at no more than the fair market value of each item in the state where the facility is located. By establishing a clear definition of fair market value and excluding prices from correctional institutions and other captive markets, the legislation would ensure incarcerated people are not charged inflated prices for basic necessities. This also comes on the back of reports that the Trump Administration hopes to privatize food service, commissary, and health care across the BOP.

“People in federal custody should not be charged more for basic necessities simply because they have no other place to buy them,” said Congresswoman Foushee. “Inflated commissary prices do not just affect incarcerated people—they also place a burden on the families who sacrifice to help their loved ones afford everyday essentials. The Stop Prison Price Gouging Act establishes a clear, commonsense standard for fair pricing, strengthens transparency and accountability, and ensures that federal prison commissaires are not used as a source of unfair profit from a captive market.”

The legislation would require the Bureau of Prisons to use competitive bidding when awarding commissary contracts and prohibit contracts that include revenue-sharing arrangements. It will also require the Bureau of Prisons to review commissary prices every month, submit an annual report to Congress detailing available goods, prices, and contracts at each facility, and undergo annual audits by the Government Accountability Office to ensure compliance with the bill’s fair-pricing requirements.

The Stop Prison Price Gouging Act of 2026 is endorsed by Brennan Center for Justice, FAMM, the Prison Policy Initiative, and the Vera Institute of Justice.

“At a prison commissary, basic necessities like soap and toothpaste should be sold at market value, not at a markup. Unfortunately, that’s not always the case in federal prison. Overcharging for things like reading glasses hurts the people who are incarcerated and, in many cases, their families who fund commissary accounts. It’s time to make it more affordable for the people behind bars to take care of themselves. This bill is about human dignity, and Congress should pass it into law,” said JC Hendrickson, senior policy strategist in the justice program at the Brennan Center for Justice.

“Incarcerated people and their families spend billions of dollars every year on commissary purchases. FAMM is proud to endorse the Stop Prison Price Gouging Act because no one should be exploited by inflated prices for basic needs such as toiletries and phone calls,” said Kevin Hagan, Esq., Federal Legislative Affairs Director with FAMM (formerly Families Against Mandatory Minimums).

"Prison Policy Initiative is happy to support the Stop Prison Price Gouging Act. People in federal prisons may earn as little as $0.12 an hour from their work assignments and are often among the poorest in the country before their incarceration. Nevertheless, they are routinely forced to pay far more for an item in prison than they would in the community. Families are left to shoulder the burden, spending an average of $4200 each year to support their loved ones during incarceration. This bill recognizes the economic burdens incarcerated people and their families often face and seeks to address them by providing much-needed guardrails for prison contracts and by ensuring that prices in prison reflect fair market value," said Sarah Staudt, Director of Advocacy and Policy at Prison Policy Initiative.

“No one should be forced to pay inflated prices for basic necessities simply because they are incarcerated. When commissary prices are too high, the burden falls not only on incarcerated people but also on the families who often sacrifice to help their loved ones afford everyday essentials. This legislation is an important step toward ensuring that federal prison commissary prices are fair, transparent, and free from profiteering,” said Aiden Cotter, Director of Federal Advocacy, Vera Institute of Justice and Vera Action.
title: Rep. Foushee Introduces Bill to End Price Gouging in Federal Prison Commissaries

WASHINGTON, DC – This week, Congresswoman Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03) authored six amendments that passed in the House as part of the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The amendments address child care access for military families, servicemember health and safety, workforce shortages in defense-adjacent industries, and next-generation manufacturing and materials research.

“If Congress is willing to spend hundreds of billions on new wars, we have a responsibility to invest in the servicemembers and veterans who bear the cost,” said Congresswoman Scholten. “My amendments do exactly that—delivering affordable child care for military families, better care for traumatic brain injuries, and critical investments in our defense workforce. I’ll keep working to get these commonsense proposals signed into law.”

The NDAA sets policy and funding priorities for the Department of Defense each year. The amendments introduced by the Congresswoman would:

Expand access to child care for military families.

Improve the diagnosis and treatment of blast-related brain injuries.

Explore innovative medical technologies that could reduce recovery times for servicemembers.

Address shortages in the aviation maintenance workforce.

Strengthen domestic tool and die manufacturing capabilities.

Study next-generation vessel materials to improve durability and readiness.

In addition to Congresswoman Scholten’s bipartisan amendments, the NDAA includes several priorities House Democrats secured, including pay raises for servicemembers, stronger support for military families, and protections for the defense workforce. However, the legislation also authorizes historically high levels of defense spending tied to the Trump Administration’s war with Iran and is paired with the SAVE Act, a partisan and restrictive voting measure.

Since the NDAA requires further improvements to strengthen its support for servicemembers, veterans, and military families while advancing responsible national security priorities, Congresswoman Scholten voted against the House-passed bill. She will advocate for the continued inclusion of her amendments and beneficial changes to the bill as it moves to the Senate for consideration.

###
title: Congresswoman Scholten Passes Six Amendments Through the House In The National Defense Authorization Act of 2027

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Congressman James R. Walkinshaw (VA-11) and Congressman James Moylan (Guam) introduced the bipartisan Military Installation Readiness and Resilience Act of 2026 to safeguard military bases from natural hazards and ensure America’s Armed Forces remain ready to respond when called.

Over the past decade, extreme weather and natural hazards caused more than $15 billion in damage at military installations, disrupting critical missions and resources that support service members and their families. A February 2026 Government Accountability Office report found that the Department of Defense (DOD) does not fully track the costs across every type of hazard, including earthquakes. Although DOD agreed that it should collect this information, it has not yet made the necessary changes.

“America’s military must be ready for every threat, including earthquakes, wildfires, and floods that can damage bases and disrupt critical missions,” said Congressman Walkinshaw. “After more than $15 billion in damage over the past decade, the Department of Defense needs a complete picture of which installations are most vulnerable. Our bipartisan bill will help protect service members, strengthen critical infrastructure, and ensure taxpayer dollars are invested where they are needed most.”

The Military Installation Readiness and Resilience Act directs the Secretary of Defense to expand DOD’s regular data collection to include the costs and effects of all natural disasters affecting military installations.

Without complete information, DOD cannot fully determine which installations face the greatest risks or where improvements are most urgently needed. By closing this critical information gap, the legislation will help protect military infrastructure, strengthen resilience, and keep America’s Armed Forces ready to carry out their mission.

Read the full bill text here.

###
title: Walkinshaw, Moylan Introduce Bipartisan Bill to Safeguard Military Bases from Natural Disasters

Toledo, OH — Earlier this month, Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09) of Northwest Ohio joined Congressman Ro Khanna (CA-17), the Ranking Member of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, in sending a bipartisan letter to the heads of US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) urging their immediate action to stop unfairly traded solar products made in China and other countries from entering the United States. These imports are undercutting American companies, including First Solar—a major employer and innovative solar panel manufacturer in Northwest Ohio.

In the last year, an incorrect customs ruling has allowed growing volumes of foreign‑made silicon wafers—popularly called “blue wafers” because they have a blue anti‑reflective coating—to enter through US ports. These wafers are being used by foreign solar manufacturers to build solar panels while avoiding customs duties meant to be applied to imported wafers.

The letter also requests clear IRS guidance be published to prevent companies using imported wafers in their solar panels from improperly claiming advanced manufacturing production tax credits for solar panel production. Congress authorized these tax credits to support US manufacturers that produce components and solar panels here in the United States—not for companies using nearly finished foreign‑made parts.

“The intentional import into the US of nearly finished solar cells made in countries that skirt our trade laws and harm American workers must stop. If these products enter our country, they should pay antidumping and countervailing duties and should not qualify for tax credits reserved for domestic manufacturers,” said Congresswoman Kaptur (OH‑09). “Northwest Ohio is home to First Solar, which has worked closely with the University of Toledo and leads the industry in advanced thin‑film technology. I will never stop working to ensure full and fair enforcement of US trade and tax laws that protect American companies, jobs, and workers—no matter where the threat comes from.”

Joining Congresswoman Kaptur and Congressman Khanna on their bipartisan letter were Republican Congressman Mike Bost (IL-10) and Republican Congressman Pat Harrigan (NC-10). The letter follows a site visit made by Congresswoman Kaptur and Congressman Khanna to First Solar’s Perrysburg facilities in May, where they met with workers and company leaders to discuss Federal policies that support American manufacturing and protect US jobs. The letter is part of ongoing efforts to strengthen the domestic solar industry in partnership with the Solar Energy Manufacturers for America Coalition (SEMA).

First Solar, founded in 1999, operates three advanced manufacturing and research facilities in Ohio, including in Perrysburg, employing over 1,600 workers. The company reports that its Ohio operations support an estimated 9,360 direct, indirect, and induced jobs statewide, generating approximately $792 Million in labor income. In addition, First Solar’s operations added roughly $1.23 Billion in value to Ohio’s economy and produced more than $4.25 Billion in total economic output in 2025.

# # #
title: Kaptur Calls on Trump Administration to Step Up Enforcement of Trade and Tax Laws to Protect America’s Domestic Solar Energy Manufacturers

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Representative Jan Schakowsky (IL-09) and U.S. Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) reintroduced bicameral legislation to reduce housing accessibility barriers and improve mobility for people with disabilities. The Eleanor Smith Inclusive Home Design Act would require all newly constructed single-family homes, townhouses and multi-level dwelling units built with federal funding include at least one accessible (or “zero step”) entrance into the home, doorways wide enough for a wheelchair on the main level and one wheelchair accessible bathroom, as well as light switches and thermostats at reachable heights from a wheelchair.

“The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) helped expand opportunity for millions of Americans, but our work is far from over,” said Congresswoman Jan Schakowsky. “I am proud to once again join Senator Duckworth in introducing the Eleanor Smith Inclusive Home Design Act to ensure federally assisted homes are built with accessibility in mind from the start. This commonsense legislation will help more people live safely and independently because everyone deserves a home where they can age in place with dignity."

“Over 15 percent of households are home to someone with a physical disability but only six percent of all homes actually meet accessibility standards—that’s unacceptable,” said Senator Tammy Duckworth. “Veterans, seniors and people with disabilities deserve to be able to move around their own homes and visit friends and family without worrying about architectural barriers, and I’m proud to work alongside Congresswoman Schakowsky to help make homes and communities more accessible for everyone.”

The Eleanor Smith Inclusive Home Design Act would require all newly built federally funded single-family homes, townhouses, modular homes and multi-level dwelling units incorporate “visitability” principles: at least one zero step entrance; doorways wide enough for a wheelchair on main level; one wheelchair accessible bathroom; and light switches and thermostats at reachable heights. According to findings in HUD’s 2019 American Housing Survey, 23.1 million households—or about one in five—are home to at least one individual with accessibility needs, and 9.2 million of those households require stairs to access the home and do not have ramps or lifts of some type. As our population continues to age rapidly, it is important to address our insufficient supply of visitable homes. Remodeling a home to include accessibility features costs more than $4,000 on average, which is significantly more expensive than the cost of incorporating these features in the initial construction process.

Schakowsky and Duckworth first introduced identical House and Senate legislation in the 116th Congress. The bill is named after Eleanor Smith, a leader in the thirty-year movement to ensure that all new homes are visitable by mobility-impaired individuals. Smith has successfully secured accessibility requirements in local building codes across the country, however federal accessibility requirements are still nonexistent for privately-owned homes.

The American Association of Interior Designers, Autism Society, Disability Rights Education & Defense Fund, Independence First, National Council on Independent Living, Paralyzed Veterans of America, the Arc of the United States, National Low Income Housing Coalition, the Kelsey and Justice in Aging all support the Eleanor Smith Inclusive Home Design Act.

###
title: Schakowsky, Duckworth Lead Bill to Provide Accessible Housing for Veterans, Individuals with Disabilities and Aging Americans

(Washington, DC) – U.S. Congressman Ed Case (HI-01) Tuesday voted in the full U.S. House against the current version of the $1.15 trillion Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

The annual authorization is considered must-pass legislation, with Congress enacting one every year since fiscal 1962. It is separate from the regular annual appropriations bills that Representative Case helps develop as a member of the House Appropriations Committee; those bills actually direct funding using the NDAA as an authorizing framework.

“Our National Defense Authorization Act is a critical annual measure that not only authorizes our defense spending for the year, supplementing my Appropriations Committee’s parallel funding responsibilities, but also establishes defense policies, including organization and administration of the Defense Department,” said Case, who serves on the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, responsible for all defense and intelligence community funding, and previously served on the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, responsible for all funding in those areas.

“While this current version of the FY 2027 NDAA includes many critical Hawai‘i and Indo-Pacific priorities I requested, I regrettably had to vote against it at this stage for various reasons. These included the lack of any Congressional authorization of the Iran war; the insufficiency of any justification for the huge authorized increase in defense spending; the lack of any assurance of adequate Congressional oversight of that spending; and the inclusion of various other proposals not relevant to defense such as the SAVE America Act, which I have separately voted against several other times.”

Given the significant economic contribution of military construction to Hawai‘i, Case highlighted various projects he advocated for that were included in the NDAA, including:

· $507 million to continue building Dry Dock 5 at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam.

· $248 million to continue building the Red Hill Water Treatment Plant. Case provided the initial funding for this effort in FY 2026 through his assignment on the House Appropriations Committee.

· $184 million to expand the Ford Island Pacific Warfighting Center at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam.

· $142 million to make airfield improvements at the Pacific Missile Range Facility.

· $90 million for an aircraft maintenance hangar at Wheeler Army Airfield.

· $77 million to expand an armory at Marine Corps Base Hawai‘i.

· $72 million for water wells and storage tanks at Helemano Military Reservation.

· $71 million for a clear well and booster pump at Fort Shafter.

· $49 million to upgrade the main gate at Marine Corp Base Hawai‘i.

· $34 million at Marine Corps Base Hawai‘i for an air traffic control compound.

· $30 million for a fire station at Schofield Barracks.

· $26 million for an elevated water tank and distribution lines at Schofield Barracks.

· $21 million for a water storage tank Schofield Barracks.

· $4 million for a Secure Integration Support Lab on Maui.

The measure also included three floor amendments (amendments added in full House deliberations) authored by Case that:

· Require a study on the potential benefits of establishing a Strategic Infrastructure Partnership Initiative to assist U.S. Pacific Command (USPACOM) in identifying, developing and implementing dual-use infrastructure projects across the Indo-Pacific.

· Require a comprehensive analysis of the People's Republic of China's (PRC) influence and activities within the Freely Associated States and recommending steps to help protect these three Pacific nations.

· Direct the Space Force to assess the security, physical, cyber and geopolitical vulnerabilities of commercially owned and operated satellite ground-based nodes located within the Indo-Pacific. Multiple such locations are in Hawai‘i.

The bill further included several provisions advocated for and supported by Case to continue the military’s investment in Hawai‘i and the Indo-Pacific, including:

· Authorizing an additional $2.5 million for the Pacific Disaster Center on Maui.

· Extending the authority for the Pacific Deterrence Initiative.

· Formally establishing an Inter-Pacific Air Forces Academy. This existing yet uncodified program focuses on leader-follower self-awareness, enhancing strategic intelligence, cultivating intercultural communication and fostering relationships among the multinational enlisted force.

· Requiring a study on recapitalizing the Army’s watercraft fleet and how they will be supported by uncrewed systems. Hawai‘i is the homeport for three Army watercraft.

· Directing the military to prioritize the distribution and retention of KC-135 tanker aircraft to Air Force and Air National Guard installations in the Indo-Pacific. Hawai‘i Air National Guard’s 154th Wing currently operates KC-135s out of Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam.

· Requiring the military to establish a secure, all-domain, virtual-constructive training environment to support training in the Indo-Pacific. This will help reduce the need to conduct more dangerous live-fire training.

· Directing the Navy to evaluate installations that are critical to force generation, deployment and sustainment for USPACOM and what can be done to improve the capacity of naval shipyards, regional maintenance centers, depots, aircraft maintenance facilities and civilian industrial capacity to maintain, repair and rearm ships and aircraft.

· Authorizing $1 billion for the Taiwan Security Cooperation Initiative.

· Authorizing $8.4 billion for two Virginia-class attack submarines. Pearl Harbor is the home of this class of submarine and conducts major maintenance on them at the Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard.

The bill additionally included several provisions cosponsored by Case, including amendments that:

· Direct the Defense Department to conduct base hardening assessments at key logistics nodes and commercial interfaces for major defense installations, which would include locations in Hawai‘i.

· Direct the military to inventory, assess and prioritize all military construction and logistics infrastructure projects across the Indo-Pacific to meet USPACOM’s operational requirements.

· Extend the requirement to annually assess of Taiwan’s military readiness, regional allied responses and U.S. contingency planning in the face of rising Chinese aggression.

· Extend the Indo-Pacific Maritime Security Initiative through 2031 and expand it to include unmanned systems.

· Mandate a report to Congress on the military’s strategy for developing a resilient and distributed missile tracking system and authorize funds to implement the report’s recommendations. These efforts can be used to help improve the defense of Hawai‘i.

Finally, the NDAA version included various provisions Case has supported to assist our nation’s servicemembers, including:

· Directs a 7% pay raise for junior enlisted personnel, a 6% raise for senior enlisted personnel and junior officers, and a 5% raise for senior officers.

· Protects the collective bargaining rights of civilian Defense Department employees.

· Authorizes over $1.8 billion for new construction of barracks and family housing.

· Requires an assessment of junior enlisted housing shortfalls and a plan to close housing shortfalls.

· Authorizes incentive pay for medical officers with doctoral degrees.

· Increases the Family Separation Allowance for deployed servicemembers.

· Authorizes $226 million to design and build new childcare centers.

· Authorizes $170 million for new on-base schools.

· Authorizes a pilot program to provide grants to expand access to childcare for military families.

· Authorizes $50 million in Impact Aid assistance to public schools with military dependent students and an additional $20 million in assistance to local schools teaching children with severe disabilities.

· Requires a cost-of-living allowance to eligible servicemembers. The authority is currently optional and only applies to servicemembers assigned to high-cost areas.

The bill passed the House by a vote of 216 to 212 and now heads to the Senate for its consideration. “I am hopeful that, as this critical measure moves further through the legislative process, its serious flaws will be corrected and I will be able to vote yes on the final version, as I have with past NDAAs,” said Case.

WASHINGTON – Congressman Steve Cohen (TN-9) today announced that St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital will receive two grants from the National Cancer Institute and that the University of Memphis will receive one grant from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.

One of the St. Jude grants, for $622,500, is for research on transcriptional regulation in ZFTA-RELA ependymoma under the direction of Dr. Mark C. Mack in the Department of Developmental Neurobiology. The second St. Jude grant, for $289,893, is for research on a treatment for pediatric patients with relapsed refractory sarcomas under the direction of Dr. Rebecca Epperly, a faculty member in the Department of Bone Marrow Transplantation and Cellular Therapy.

The University of Memphis grant, for $53,114, is for research into alcohol use by non-four-year college emerging adults, under the direction of clinical psychology doctoral student Jacob Tempchin.

Congressman Cohen made the following statement:

“St. Jude researchers are improving patient outcomes with the kinds of work these grants will underwrite. Understanding alcoholic behavior in young people is also likely to improve outcomes. I congratulate Drs. Mack and Epperly and Mr. Tempchin for the valuable work they’re doing.”

USPS Reverses Course and Will Provide Curbside Service to the Squire Drive and Piedmont Street Subdivision, Nearly a Year After Kennedy Demanded Action from the Postmaster General

WHEATFIELD, N.Y. — Congressman Tim Kennedy (NY-26) announced that the United States Postal Service (USPS) has begun to provide curbside mail delivery to residents of the Whistling Straits subdivision in the Town of Wheatfield, ending years of frustration in which homeowners were forced to rely on P.O. boxes while every surrounding street received service at the curb. The decision follows a letter Kennedy sent to the Postmaster General in August 2025 requesting an exemption from USPS's cluster mailbox policy for the roughly 35-home development.

“This is what happens when neighbors and their elected officials work together and refuse to take no for an answer,” said Congressman Kennedy. “Whistling Straits residents deserved the same mail service as every family on the surrounding streets all along, and now they'll finally have it. I want to thank USPS for reconsidering, and I'll keep fighting to make sure Western New Yorkers get the services they deserve.”

“The Town of Wheatfield has been trying to resolve this issue for years, and we're grateful to Congressman Kennedy for his help in getting it done,” said Wheatfield Town Supervisor Don MacSwan. “Thanks to the persistence of our Town Board, our local postmaster, and everyone who worked to make this happen, our residents will finally get the same delivery service as their neighbors around the block, which is all they ever asked for.”

Whistling Straits, made up of Squire Drive and Piedmont Street, received local planning approval before USPS's 2012 shift to cluster mailboxes as the default for new developments. Because the subdivision has no homeowners association and no sidewalks, residents and Town officials had argued a cluster mailbox posed both a maintenance and a winter-safety concern. Kennedy's letter noted the development is bounded by Ward Road, Hoover Road, and Lockport Road, all of which already receive curbside delivery.

###
title: Kennedy Announces Beginning of Curbside Mail Delivery for Whistling Straits Residents in Wheatfield

Today, Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher (TX-07) joined Congressional Hispanic Caucus Chair Adriano Espaillat, House Committee on Homeland Security Ranking Member Bennie Thompson, and Congresswoman Sylvia Garcia (TX-29) for an oversight forum on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) use of force and abuse of power, following the tragic killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by ICE in Houston on July 7, 2026.

The forum, entitled “Seeking Justice: Oversight of ICE’s Use of Force in the Death of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo,” included testimony from Lorenzo Salgado Araujo’s sons, Ronaldo Salgado Araujo and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo Jr.; Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare; Houston City Council Member Joaquin Martinez (District I); LULAC President & CEO Juan Proaño; East End Communities Director Patricia Cabrera; and Immaculate Conception Catholic Church Rev. Salvatore De George.

Congresswoman Fletcher’s oversight forum remarks as delivered:

Congresswoman Fletcher:

Well thank you, Chairman Espaillat, and thanks to you and Ranking Member Thompson and Representative Garcia for convening this important oversight forum. And I want to thank all of my colleagues who've come from across the country to see and hear from our community. And I want to thank our witnesses from our community for so beautifully explaining and showing this community to the rest of the country. Because people across our community and across the country, as Father De George and Ms. Cabrera explained so beautifully, have been living in fear. And their worst fears were realized again when federal agents killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. So I want to thank all of you for testifying and for your leadership in our community, especially at this devastating time.

Ronaldo and Lorenzo, my thoughts have been and will continue to be with you and your mother and your entire family, not just today, but in all the days ahead. You make us proud, and you make us all proud for your advocacy and for your commitment to justice for all. And I hope today's hearing will demonstrate to you and to everyone here our commitment of not only our Houston Congressional Democratic Delegation, but the Congressional Hispanic Caucus and the entire House Democratic Caucus.

It is a failure of this Congress—and many before—that we have not been able to pass laws to address our broken immigration system. The people here have been trying and will continue to do so, but it is a new and utter failure of this Republican-controlled Congress that has not only failed to address—it has refused to address the abuses that this White House is directing in terms of immigration enforcement operations. And that it has done nothing—nothing—when innocent people in this country have been killed at the hands of federal immigration agents this year and during this term.

It is a betrayal of families and communities across the country that we represent. It is a betrayal of the Constitution that we have all sworn an oath to protect and defend, and it is a betrayal of our values as Americans. And yet, what we hear from those who are directing these policies is that these actions are being taken to make us safe. And so, District Attorney Teare, I want to direct my questions—start my questions—with you. Can you tell us from your experience of 20 years in law enforcement whether the policies that we have seen implemented at ICE—and in terms of immigration enforcement throughout DHS—in the last 18 months have made our communities safer?

District Attorney Teare:

Objectively, no. They've had the complete opposite effect.

Congresswoman Fletcher:

And can you tell us why that is? Can you give us some examples of what is making us less safe because of the policies that this administration is implementing?

District Attorney Teare:

We have people who are here unauthorized, who are victims of domestic violence, aggravated robbery, aggravated sexual assault, who are too scared to even call the police, let alone participate in prosecutions of people who are here with documentation or who are citizens. These policies have effectively created a group of our community that are targets, and that's what we're seeing.

And we can't hold the people that prey on them accountable. And that group of people knows it.

Congresswoman Fletcher:

Thank you. In addition, Mr. Green asked about dash cams, and I also want to ask about the increased presence of unmarked vehicles and plainclothes officers for immigration enforcement activities. That's something I know many of us up here have objected to repeatedly, but can you talk about what that does in our communities as well?

District Attorney Teare:

Yeah. It continues the feeling of fear—the floating fear that Father talked about. But it's just not good law enforcement policy. Undercover work is crucial to good law enforcement policy. But undercover officers don't then affect the traffic stops for reasons that we have seen time and again around the fear of the person trying to be stopped. So it is not best practices.

Congresswoman Fletcher:

Thank you. And with the time I have left, Council Member Martinez, I just want to direct this question to you. Can you share with us how you see in the community this affects interactions with law enforcement agencies that come under your jurisdiction, like the Houston Police Department and others, and in the community because of the actions of these federal officers?

Council Member Martinez:

Yes, Congresswoman. So it's important to continue to highlight that calls for services are down. My team, we've done some research. We've gotten data from HPD within our zip codes. And they have gone down. And then even heavier in the southwest part of Houston, where we have an even more diverse immigrant population, called them services have gone down even more. So what we're finding as well is that, when residents—and I've shared my personal number with several community folks—when something is happening, an operation is happening, and folks can’t identify who is heading that operation, we're having to call and figure out what agency this is

in order to try and tamper down those fears.

Congresswoman Fletcher:

Thank you, Council Member, I've gone over my time, I appreciate it. Thank you all for your testimony and for your work. And thank you again for convening this hearing. And I yield back.
title: ICYMI: Congresswoman Lizzie Fletcher, Members of Congress Question ICE's Use of Force Following Killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries issued the following statement after Congressman Cleo Fields announced his decision not to seek re-election to the House of Representatives:

Throughout his distinguished career in public service, Representative Cleo Fields has always fought to make life better for the people of Louisiana.

A son of Baton Rouge, Cleo was elected to the Louisiana State Senate on three occasions, becoming the youngest State Senator in Louisiana history. In 1992, Cleo was elected to Congress as the youngest Member of his class, and he rejoined us in the House last year, once again becoming a beloved member of the Congressional Black Caucus family. During his time in Congress, Rep. Fields has co-chaired the Congressional Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Caucus, been a fierce advocate for voting rights and fought to expand economic opportunity.

After being gerrymandered out of his seat in 1996, Rep. Fields founded the Congressional Classroom, a first-of-its-kind program to teach high school students about the federal government. It was an honor and a privilege to join Rep. Fields in Baton Rouge last year, where I witnessed firsthand the powerful impact of what is now called the Louisiana Leadership Institute.

On two separate occasions, Republicans have deployed undemocratic gerrymandering tactics to target and wipe out districts represented by Rep. Fields and deny equal representation to Black Louisianans. House Democrats will continue our fight to deliver fair Congressional maps, defend the integrity of our elections and end voter suppression once and for all.

Rep. Fields will be deeply missed by the entire House Democratic Caucus. We wish him and his family well during this next chapter in his lifelong service to the people of Louisiana.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Representatives Doris Matsui (D-CA) and Zach Nunn (R-IA), and Senators Mark Warner (D-VA) and Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) reintroduced the Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act, bipartisan and bicameral legislation to help schools defend against ransomware, data breaches, and other cyberattacks that can expose students’ information, disrupt classroom learning, and strain already limited school resources.

“When I thought about my own grandchildren going to school, I wanted what every parent and grandparent wants: for them to be safe and focused on learning,” said Congresswoman Matsui. “No family should have to worry that a cyberattack could expose a child’s personal information or disrupt their education. This bill gives schools the tools, training, and support they need to protect students’ data, help teachers keep classrooms running, and give administrators stronger resources to prevent and respond to cyberattacks.”

“As a 20-year Air Force intelligence officer and former White House National Security Council member, I’ve spent my whole career tracking threats like these,” said Congressman Nunn. “Now they're hitting our classrooms — shutting schools down and putting Iowa students’ personal information in the wrong hands. No school should have to fight that alone. Our bipartisan bill gives K-12 schools across the country the backup they need to stop these attacks and protect their students.”

“As cyberattacks grow more frequent and sophisticated, it’s our responsibility as lawmakers to ensure our schools have the tools and resources needed to protect students, parents, educators, and their sensitive information from being compromised,” said Senator Warner. “Schools should be focused on teaching young people – not worried about fending off ransomware attacks or recovering from cyber incidents. I’m proud to reintroduce this legislation that would help school districts strengthen their cyber defenses, improve coordination with federal experts, and better prepare for the growing threats facing classrooms across the country.”

“Cyberattacks continue to grow in size, frequency, and complexity in critical U.S. institutions, including in America’s schools,” said Senator Blackburn. “We must ensure that our education sector is equipped to address these threats and keep students’ personal information private. This bipartisan and bicameral legislation will improve the cybersecurity tracking system for schools and provide them with necessary training resources and best practices for prevention.”

Cyberattacks targeting K-12 schools continue to grow in both frequency and sophistication, exposing sensitive student information, disrupting classroom learning, and forcing schools to divert limited resources away from educating students. According to the 2025 Center for Internet Security (CIS) K-12 Cybersecurity Report, 82% of more than 5,000 K-12 organizations experienced cyber threat impacts between July 2023 and December 2024, underscoring the growing challenge schools face as they rely more heavily on digital technologies.

Federal cybersecurity officials have repeatedly warned that schools remain targets for ransomware and other malicious cyber activity because they often operate with limited cybersecurity personnel and budgets while maintaining large amounts of sensitive data. The Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act would help schools better prepare for these threats by improving access to cybersecurity guidance and resources, strengthening national awareness of cyber incidents affecting schools, and expanding the tools and support available to help school systems.

The Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act would:

Establish a School Cybersecurity Information Exchange

Directs the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Director to establish a Cybersecurity Information Exchange to disseminate information, best practices, and grant opportunities to improve cybersecurity.

Create a Cybersecurity Incident Registry

Establishes a Cybersecurity Incident Registry within CISA to track incidents of cyberattacks on elementary and secondary schools. Information submitted to the Registry is strictly voluntary and will help improve data collection to coordinate activities related to the nationwide monitoring of the incidence and financial impact of cyberattacks.

Launch a K-12 Cybersecurity Technology Improvement Program

Directs CISA to establish the K-12 Cybersecurity Technology Improvement Program to be administered through an information and analysis organization to deploy cybersecurity capabilities that will help address cybersecurity risks and threats to information systems of K-12 schools. This approach will capitalize on the existing services and expertise of organizations like MS-ISAC & others to ensure maximum impact of funds. The legislation authorizes $10 million annually for fiscal years 2027 and 2028 to fund the Technology Improvement Program.

Full text of the Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act can be found HERE.

The Sacramento County Office of Education, National Principals Association, National Association of Elementary School Principals, Council of Chief State School Officers, National Association of State Chief Information Officers, State Educational Technology Directors Association, and Consortium for School Networking endorsed the legislation.

“As a local educational agency that provides internet connectivity to 250,000 students across California, the Sacramento County Office of Education sees firsthand the growing threat that cyberattacks pose to student information, instructional continuity, and school operations,” said Jerry Jones, executive director of Technology Resources for the Sacramento County Office of Education.“This bill would provide much-needed, practical support to schools by expanding access to K–12-specific cybersecurity guidance, training, cybersecurity information, funding opportunities, and effective tools and services. Its emphasis on improving coordination, strengthening protections against ransomware and other cyber threats, and helping schools learn from cyber incidents recognizes that schools should not have to face these increasingly sophisticated attacks alone. I strongly support this important legislation and its commitment to strengthening the security and resilience of our nation’s schools.”

“Schools are increasingly at risk from cybersecurity threats. NAESP is proud to endorse the Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act, a bill which would give our members practical tools, information, and resources from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to help pre-K-8 school leaders protect student data and privacy and to avoid costly school disruptions,” said L. Earl Franks, executive director of the National Association of Elementary School Principals. “We commend Representatives Matsui and Nunn and Senators Blackburn and Warner for their bipartisan leadership on this critically important issue.”

“Cybersecurity remains one of the most urgent technology challenges facing K-12 schools. School districts face increasingly sophisticated cyber threats that can disrupt learning, compromise student and personnel data, and strain already limited technology resources,” said Keith Krueger, CEO of the Consortium for School Networking (CoSN). “CoSN strongly supports the bipartisan Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act because it will strengthen information sharing, improve understanding of the cyber threats facing schools, and expand access to the resources and expertise districts need to better protect their networks. We applaud the bill's bicameral and bipartisan sponsors for their leadership on this important issue.”
title: MATSUI INTRODUCES BIPARTISAN LEGISLATION TO STRENGTHEN CYBERSECURITY IN K-12 SCHOOLS

Queens, NY – U.S. Rep. Gregory W. Meeks (NY-05) and a broad coalition of faith leaders, local elected officials, labor organizations, and Haitian community advocates hosted a press conference calling on the U.S. Senate to pass legislation extending Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians through January 29, 2029. This press conference comes shortly after a federal appeals court temporarily blocked the revocation of TPS for Haitians, extending protections and work authorizations until July 27, 2026.

Despite the clear and present dangers to those living in Haiti, the Supreme Court ruled in the Trump Administration’s favor, allowing them to terminate TPS for over 330,000 Haitians in the United States. Violent crime and kidnapping are rampant, armed groups terrorize entire communities and hospitals lack basic resources. Recognizing these dangerous conditions, the U.S. State Department continues to maintain its highest travel advisory for Haiti – Level 4 “Do Not Travel.” TPS was created for moments exactly like this – when conditions in a country make a safe return impossible.

Image

“For generations, Haitian immigrants helped write New York’s story and built thriving communities across Queens,” said Congressman Gregory Meeks. “They are the parents of over 50,000 U.S. children nationwide, and community members who contribute over $1 billion to the New York City economy each year. Yet the Trump Administration chose to end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians—even as Haiti remains consumed by gang violence, displacement, hunger, and political collapse. That is why I voted to pass legislation to extend TPS for Haiti and continue to call on the U.S. Senate to do the same. Our fight isn’t over yet.”

Congressman Meeks and House Democrats successfully forced a vote on legislation extending TPS for Haiti for three years. On April 16, 2026, the measure passed the House of Representatives by a vote of 224 to 204, with total Democratic support and 10 Republicans breaking away from their party. The measure now awaits consideration in the U.S. Senate. Constituents of New York’s 5th Congressional District in need of assistance with federal casework may contact Congressman Meeks’ Jamaica District Office at (718) 725-6000.
title: Rep. Meeks, Faith Leaders, Local Elected Officials, Labor and Community Organizations Fight for Haitian TPS Extension

Above: Gottheimer announces $42 million+ in funding to New Jersey.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, July 24, 2026, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) and the White House announced more than $42 million in Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) funding to strengthen law enforcement and keep Jersey communities safe. This funding comes on top of the $8.5 million previously secured to protect Jersey during the World Cup, totaling more than $50 million clawed back for New Jersey law enforcement since June.

Watch Gottheimer’s announcement here.

Half of the new funding clawed back today — $21 million — will go statewide, to support New Jersey public safety, including State Police, defraying World Cup related expenditures, and other public safety and transit measures up and down the state.

The other half — $21 million — is going directly to New Jersey’s Fifth Congressional District, for public safety in Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties, including local and county law enforcement efforts, transit security, and security for houses of worship and religious schools.

Breakdown of Funds and Their Use:

Gear for cops on the ground: Allows local and state police to invest in updated radios, drones, gear for active shooter and mass-casualty response, and K-9 training.

Protecting places of worship: Provides security upgrades like armed guards, cameras, reinforced doors, fencing, and more for synagogues, churches, mosques, temples, and other nonprofits. Jersey families shouldn’t have to think twice about safety when they go to their place of worship.

Securing transportation hubs: Adds additional security cameras, cybersecurity protections, and physical reinforcement of the Andover train station. This project that Gottheimer has championed for years, will bring rail back to Sussex County for the first time in over 50 years. These added security dollars will help avoid any delays in getting this critical station open.

“Today, building on that, and working with the White House, I am proud to announce that we have clawed back more than $42 million in FEMA grant funding from Washington, DC to New Jersey for public safety right here in Jersey’s Fifth Congressional District. Every single day, rain or shine, late nights, early mornings, weekends, holidays, kids’ birthdays and other family occasions, you put on the uniform, and you respond without hesitation. You get our backs. And I want you to know, as ever, that I’ll always get yours,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “The men and women who wear the badge go above and beyond to protect us, and they’ve earned every bit of support we can give them — for the big events and the everyday calls alike. That’s what this funding is about. I went to bat in Washington, and after months of negotiations and relentless advocacy, I clawed back more than $42 million home to Jersey and put it exactly where it belongs: in the hands of the brave men and women keeping our communities safe.”

“Keeping New Jersey families safe starts with making sure our first responders have the resources they need to do their jobs. Our congressional delegation is essential in delivering federal dollars that help strengthen public safety in communities across our state, and I want to thank Congressman Gottheimer for helping secure this funding for New Jersey. For too long, New Jerseyans have sent far more to Washington than we receive in return. This investment is a step toward ensuring our taxpayers see more of their hard-earned dollars come back home to support our first responders,” said Governor Mikie Sherrill.

Resources will flow to the New Jersey Office of Homeland Security and Preparedness through several grants, including the State Homeland Security Program (SHSP),; the Urban Area Security Initiative (UASI); the Emergency Management Performance Grant (EMPG); the Transit Security Grant Program (TSGP); and the Nonprofit Security Grant Program (NSGP). These resources are dedicated to disaster prevention, supporting the law enforcement and security operations that keep our communities safe and secure.

Gottheimer was joined by Bergen County Prosecutor Mark Musella; Passaic County Prosecutor Camilla Valdes; Sussex County Prosecutor Dan Perez; Bergen County Executive Jim Tedesco III; Senator Gordon Johnson; Assemblywoman Lisa Swain; Fort Lee Mayor Mark Sokolich; Newton Mayor Matthew Dickson; Fair Lawn Mayor Cristinie Cutrone; Englewood Cliffs Mayor Mark Park; Englewood Mayor Michael Wildes; Ringwood Mayor Jamie Landis; Lafayette Mayor Richard Hughes; Ho-Ho-Kus Mayor Thomas Randall; Vernon Mayor Anthony Rossi; Wanaque Mayor Dan Mahler; Bloomingdale Mayor John D’Amato; Andover Deputy Mayor Krista Ghilcrist; Ringwood Councilwoman Yvonne M. Echols; Tenafly Borough Administrator David Fanslau; Wanaque Borough Administrator Rob Hermansen; Tenafly Borough Clerk Omar Stovall; and Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex County first responders.

Below: Gottheimer announces $42 million+ in funding to New Jersey.

###

Gottheimer’s remarks as prepared for delivery:

Good morning, everyone.

First, I want to start by thanking the hard-working people standing here with us today. Jersey’s finest.

Our local police departments. Our sheriffs and county prosecutors and their teams. Our state troopers. Our firefighters and our EMS crews. Everyone who answers the call, no matter the hour.

You roll up on a call at two in the morning, not knowing what’s on the other side of that door. You chase down a stolen car through a school zone. You answer a 911 call for help because someone’s having a heart attack. You stand post for hours outside a house of worship because a threat came in overnight. The job never slows down, and the risks just keep getting bigger.

Every single day, rain or shine, late nights, early mornings, weekends, holidays, kids’ birthdays and other family occasions, you put on the uniform and you respond without hesitation. You get our backs. And I want you to know, as ever, that I’ll always get yours.

Far too often, our local and county police departments — the men and women protecting the towns you live in, whether that’s in Bergen, Passaic, or Sussex Counties — have been stretched thin, without all the resources they need to protect our families and themselves.

Updated radios and communication systems. Specialty drones. Additional K-9 units. Gear for the worst-case scenarios nobody wants to think about — and all of the training that goes along with it. It’s all expensive. But the truth is that you want them to have it.

Why? Thanks to our phenomenal law enforcement and prosecutors, crime is down in Jersey with a 30% drop in statewide shootings and a 6% overall crime rate reduction over the last year. Auto thefts are down 9% since 2024 due to coordinated federal, state, and local action, but more needs to be done.

Just this past June, our NJ cops busted more than 60 criminals involved in an $8 million auto theft ring that stole more than 90 cars by breaking into homes for key fobs and then shipping the cars to West Africa. Other auto thieves are changing their tactics to steal sensors and airbags out of cars parked on the street to sell on the black market. Cyber theft is also surging across New Jersey, with victims losing more than $435 million, ranking Jersey 5th nationwide for total losses to cybercrime. And organized retail crime continues to be a problem in our state, with highly professional groups targeting our local businesses to seize merchandise that they sell for a profit.

Thanks to social media, cable news, and massive disinformation, one area that has moved in the wrong direction is hate crimes, especially those that are religiously motivated.

Houses of worship, like synagogues, churches, mosques, and temples, are facing elevated threats both in Jersey and across the country. In fact, according to the ADL, Jersey had the third-most antisemitic incidents of any state in the country, with Bergen County having the highest number in the state.

People are being attacked walking to temple, like the young man shot with a pellet gun in Teaneck earlier this year. We saw the horrific attack in New York City just yesterday, with a man screaming “Allahu akbar” as he stabbed a parishioner walking out of a synagogue. Churches, synagogues, schools, and other houses of worship have had to spend their own money, out of their own pockets, when federal dollars don’t go far enough, on security officers, cameras, alarms, and reinforced doors, just so their congregants can pray safely. In the greatest country in the world, people should be able to go to church or temple without fear.

On top of that, World Cup expenses hit our local communities, county, and state — including transit, logistics, infrastructure, and overtime costs. We obviously needed it to keep our communities safe — after all, we were hosting the world, and we did an excellent job. New Jersey at its best. But I don’t want the World Cup to hit the pocketbooks of our families — or our towns. I don’t want it coming out of your state income and local property taxes. The families in Jersey shouldn’t be footing the bill for a global sporting event that FIFA and the federal government have a responsibility to fund.

The bottom line: ensuring our public safety — keeping Jersey families safe — is essential. It’s not optional. But it’s also expensive. To help cover costs, I’ve spent the last few months in Washington working overtime, not just to help cover World Cup costs, but also to do everything we can to support our first responders — to claw more of your federal tax dollars back to North Jersey, so you don’t have to pick up the tab on your state and local taxes. Months of meetings. Months of calls. Months of negotiations. I worked with the White House and with FEMA to make sure Jersey, and especially the towns right here in the 5th District, got the funds we deserve.

In June, I proudly announced that I had clawed back $8.5 million to help cover World Cup law enforcement overtime costs for cops across Bergen County and in and around MetLife — including millions for our state police.

Today, building on that, and working with the White House, I am proud to announce that we have clawed back more than $42 million in FEMA grant funding from Washington, DC to New Jersey for public safety right here in Jersey’s Fifth Congressional District.

My dad told me a long time ago: you don’t get it if you don’t ask — and if you don’t fight hard for what’s yours. Well, I’ve also said that I’ll work with the other side if it’s good for Jersey. Protecting our towns and our state is good for Jersey; standing by law enforcement is good for Jersey; protecting our synagogues and churches to protect religious freedom is good for Jersey. Making sure Jersey is safe and our families are safe is good. This is about solving real problems that our community and our families are facing.

You know what else is good? Fighting the Moocher States and clawing money back to Jersey to help get our taxes down.

Historically, Mississippi gets about $4.38 back for every dollar it sends to Washington. West Virginia gets about $4.23 back. But New Jersey? We get about 67 cents on the dollar. That’s not nearly enough for what we put in, and far too much ends up on your state and property taxes. The less that goes to other states and the more that comes to us means lower state and property taxes for Jersey families.

Keeping score for Jersey taxpayers: in under three months, between today’s $42 million and the $8.5 million for World Cup safety in June, that’s $50.5 million clawed back from Washington to Jersey to protect our families and first responders — in just three months.

That’s all about getting your taxes down and getting money away from the Moocher States.

Those are your tax dollars pouring back into our community, keeping your property taxes down and making real, local improvements for Jersey families.

Here’s how it breaks down. Half of the new funding we clawed back today — $21 million — will go statewide, to support New Jersey State Police, law enforcement efforts up and down the state, transit security, and nonprofit security. And the other half — $21 million — is coming back home to our own Fifth Congressional District, right here for public safety in Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties.

Let me tell you exactly where this money is going, and what it’s going to do.

First: part of the $42 million will go toward protecting law enforcement and our communities, including local, county, and state police, to invest in updated radios to communicate, drones, and equipment for active shooter and mass-casualty response, along with K-9s and training. It will also help towns build and improve their emergency operations centers. That will help ensure that a cop in Hackensack, an officer in Ringwood, or a deputy in Sussex County has the tools they actually need to protect Jersey families — and come home safe at the end of the shift, or when you wake up at 2 a.m. to respond to a health emergency.

These dollars will invest in emergency radio replacement for towns like Fort Lee that need to transition to modern, reliable communication systems. I know radios might not sound exciting, but they’re absolutely vital to helping our officers get the job done in our towns and across the county. When an officer chases a suspect from one town into the next, their radios have to bridge that gap. When they need an ambulance on scene, they have to reach EMS instantly — no delay, no dead air. When a fire crew backs up a neighboring department, they have to be on the same channel. That’s the difference between help getting there in time and not.

We learned that the hardest way possible. On 9/11, our first responders couldn’t communicate. Radios from different departments didn’t talk to each other, servers and radios failed in the towers, and firefighters climbing those stairwells never got the order to get out. Brave men and women died in part because the equipment failed them. We swore we’d never let that happen again, and the technology never stops changing, so neither can we.

That’s why, working hand in hand with the Bergen County Prosecutor, we’re setting up a dedicated fund for radios and communications equipment, hosted right out of the Prosecutor’s office. And we will do the same for the towns I represent in Passaic and Sussex Counties. Any town can come to us and flag that they need radios, and we’ll do our best to get you what you need — or a down payment toward it.

Second, part of the $42 million we’ve clawed back will go to protecting our houses of worship here in the Fifth Congressional District. No family should have to think twice about their safety when they walk into a synagogue, a church, a mosque, or a temple.

This funding provides real security upgrades like cameras, security guards, fences, reinforced doors, and alarm systems for our congregations and our nonprofits right here in North Jersey. And security is expensive.

Historically, thanks to our strong coordination with our houses of worship, and my relentless push in Washington, our district has clawed back the most nonprofit security grant funding of any district in Jersey. That makes sense — we have the highest number of antisemitic incidents of any district in the state.

Antisemitic incidents are up 70 percent since October 7, and hate of all kinds is thriving. Our places of worship, whether synagogues, mosques, churches, or Sikh temples, need the resources to protect their worshippers from this vile hatred, against any religion.

Third, part of the $42 million we’ve clawed back from Washington will help cover costs we got stuck with for the World Cup — which, I’ll mention again, was in Jersey, not New York, by the way. These dollars will help cover security operations, like the intelligence analysts, the traffic officers, the task force deployments, and extra emergency equipment.

Finally, part of the $42 million we clawed back today will go to securing our transportation hubs, including extra security cameras, cybersecurity protections, and physical reinforcements, including to the Andover Train Station project. These added security dollars will help avoid any delays in getting this critical station open for my constituents.

For years, I’ve pushed NJ TRANSIT and Amtrak to stop the bureaucratic delays and finally bring passenger rail back to Sussex County — and specifically Andover Train Station — for the first time in more than fifty years.

There are zero options for folks in Sussex County to get on a train to get to work or to see a family member. I’ve heard from so many residents, businesses, and local elected officials about this issue, and about the urgent need for more transportation options to New York City from across Sussex. I’ve sent letters, done site visits, and clawed millions back in the bipartisan infrastructure bill to keep Andover on the map. Now that we’re finally close to getting trains running again, the least we can do is make sure the station we fought so hard for is safe and secure from day one.

One more point: as I mentioned, half of the $42 million will help protect families and first responders across the state. I am coordinating closely with the Governor and her team to direct these dollars to the most important needs across Jersey — from State Police to our counties and towns. We will announce more specifics about those dollars in the coming weeks. That’s on top of what we’ve clawed back for Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties.

Here’s the bottom line: these are your federal tax dollars. You pay them every single year. The question is always the same: how much of that money actually comes back home to New Jersey, back to the towns you live in, instead of going somewhere else?

My job is to fight for every dollar I can, and claw it back here, where it belongs. That’s what this is: Jersey families’ own federal tax dollars, coming back home to protect Jersey — to protect our families, whether that’s in your neighborhood or at your temple or church.

This isn’t about one headline or one event. This is about the men and women who show up every single day. You’ve earned every bit of support we can give you. And there’s nothing partisan about this. This is about common sense. About solving problems. And putting our country first.

I am so proud to stand here today. I am so grateful for everything these incredible public servants do for every single one of us, every single day.

If we keep working together to support our communities, in the greatest country in the world, our best days will always be ahead of us.

Thank you, may God bless you, your families, and our first responders.
title: RELEASE: Gottheimer & White House Announce $42 Million+ in Funding From Washington to New Jersey
